en: [27.3] The Sūtra on the Merit of the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, Compassion, and World-Weariness Spoken by the Buddha;
the translator’s name is lost, now appended to the Catalogue of the Eastern Jin.
At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
There, the Buddha spoke for the sake of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada:

"In the distant past, there was a brahmin named Virama, who possessed abundant wealth and many treasures. When he practiced giving, he used eighty-four thousand golden bowls filled with crushed silver;

eighty-four thousand silver bowls filled with crushed gold; furthermore, eighty-four thousand golden and silver bathing jars; furthermore, eighty-four thousand oxen, all with horns covered in gold and silver; furthermore, eighty-four thousand noble women fully adorned with ornaments; furthermore, eighty-four thousand bedding sets covered with various colorful fabrics; furthermore, eighty-four thousand garments; furthermore, eighty-four thousand elephants and horses, all with saddles and bridles of gold and silver; and furthermore, he gave away eighty-four thousand houses."
Furthermore, one may practice giving at the four city gates, bestowing whatever others desire;
or one may give a single dwelling to the Saṃgha of the Four Quarters (cāturdisa-saṃgha).
Yet the merit from such acts of giving as described above does not equal that of receiving the Three Refuges.
The reason for this is that one who receives the Three Refuges bestows fearlessness upon all sentient beings.
Therefore, the merit of taking refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha is immeasurable.
"The merit from the aforementioned acts of giving and receiving the three refuges does not equal the merit of receiving the five precepts.
One who receives the five precepts possesses complete and perfect virtue; their merit is superior."

The merit of the aforementioned acts of giving, as well as receiving the three refuges and the five precepts, is not equal to the merit of contemplating sentient beings with loving-kindness for even the duration of a finger-snap.

Furthermore, the merit of the aforementioned giving, receiving the three refuges and five precepts, and contemplating sentient beings with loving-kindness, is not equal to the merit of giving rise to the perception that all worldly things are not to be relished.

The reason for this is that the merit arising from the perception of the unattractiveness of all worldly existence can cause the practitioner to extinguish the suffering of birth and death and ultimately achieve the Buddha-way; therefore, this merit is the most supreme.
At that time, the elder, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Merit of the Three Refuges, the Five Precepts, Compassionate Mind, and Renunciation Spoken by the Buddha.
